turns.question: can you walk me through everything that happens, at every layer, between me hitting enter on a URL and a page showing up in my browser?
turns.answer:
Six steps happen, in order. First, the browser parses the URL and checks its cache for a fresh copy of the page. Second, the browser resolves the hostname to an IP address with DNS. Third, the browser opens a TCP connection to that IP address, on port 443 for HTTPS. Fourth, the client and the server run a TLS handshake over that connection, and they agree on keys. Fifth, the browser sends an HTTP request over the encrypted connection, and the server sends back a response with a status code, headers, and a body. Sixth, the browser reads the HTML body, then it finds more resources inside it, such as images, scripts, and style sheets, and it fetches each one with its own request. The browser renders the page as the pieces arrive. It does not wait for every resource before it shows content.

This skips two layers below TCP: IP routing and the link layer that moves frames between one hop and the next. We can go into those later if you want.
turns.control:
Sure, this is the classic "what happens when you type google.com" question, and it's worth doing properly because every layer you skip is a layer you'll be debugging blind later. First your browser parses the URL and checks its own cache, then the OS resolves the hostname: local hosts file, then DNS, which itself might hit a local resolver cache, your router, your ISP's recursive resolver, and potentially a full recursive lookup through root, TLD, and authoritative servers if nothing's cached. You get back an IP.

Then the browser opens a TCP connection to that IP on port 443 (assuming HTTPS, which is almost certainly what you mean): three-way handshake, SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. On top of that TCP connection, a TLS handshake happens to establish an encrypted channel and verify the server's identity via its certificate chain. Once that's done you've got a secure pipe, and the browser sends an HTTP request over it, usually HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 these days, not plain HTTP/1.1.

The server processes the request, maybe hits a database, renders HTML, and sends back a response with headers and a body. The browser starts parsing HTML as it streams in, builds the DOM, discovers references to CSS and JS and images, and fires off more requests for those, often reusing the same connection. It builds the render tree, computes layout, paints pixels, and composites it all onto your screen. And that's the abridged version — we can go deeper on any layer, which honestly sounds like where you're headed.

turns.question: ok before we go further - what actually counts as a 'safe' http method vs an 'idempotent' one, they always get conflated
turns.answer:
A safe method does not change state on the server. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are safe. A client can send a safe request many times, or not at all, and the server stays the same.

An idempotent method can change state once, but a second identical request causes no further change. PUT and DELETE are idempotent. If you PUT the same resource twice, the resource ends in the same state it had after the first PUT.

Every safe method is also idempotent, but an idempotent method is not always safe. PUT changes state on the first call, so it is not safe, but it is idempotent because repeats do not change the result further. POST is neither safe nor idempotent by default, because two identical POST requests can create two different records.
turns.control:
Yeah, they get conflated constantly because people assume "safe" and "idempotent" are just two words for "doesn't break anything," but they're answering different questions.

Safe means the method isn't supposed to change server state at all — it's read-only as far as the spec is concerned. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are safe. The idea is you should be able to fire off a safe request without worrying that you just triggered a side effect, which is why things like prefetching and link crawlers assume it's fine to hit GET endpoints speculatively. If your GET endpoint increments a counter or deletes something, you've violated the contract, even if it "works."

Idempotent means making the same request multiple times produces the same end state as making it once. It says nothing about whether state changes, only about whether repeating the call changes anything further. GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS are idempotent. PUT /users/5 with a given body sets that resource to that exact state — call it once or ten times, user 5 ends up the same. DELETE /users/5 is idempotent too: first call deletes it, every call after is still "user 5 doesn't exist," so the end state doesn't change even though the request technically "did" something each time (some servers will 404 on the repeats, some return 204 every time — technically a gray area in practice, but the intent is idempotent).

POST is neither safe nor idempotent — calling it twice can create two resources. That's the one to be careful retrying automatically.

turns.question: so if PUT is idempotent, why do people still get burned retrying a failed PUT request automatically?
turns.answer:
Idempotent describes the method's effect on the resource, not the reliability of the network. A PUT request can succeed on the server, but the response can get lost on the way back to the client. The client then sees a timeout, and it retries. The retry sends the same PUT again, and this part is safe, because the end state still matches what the first PUT set.

The risk sits in what the client does around the retry, not in the PUT itself. If a second system depends on a side effect tied to the request, such as a webhook that fires once per received request rather than once per state change, the retry can trigger that side effect twice. Also, if two different clients retry against the same resource at the same time, the last write wins, and one client's update silently overwrites the other client's update. Idempotency guards the resource's final state. It does not guard against a race between two writers, or a side effect that is not idempotent itself.
turns.control:
Because idempotent is a property of the intended semantics, not a guarantee about what actually happens on a real network with a real server. A few ways this bites people:

The request can partially succeed. Say your PUT updates a resource and also fires a webhook or writes to two tables, and the connection drops after the first write but before the response comes back. You retry, thinking "it's idempotent, no harm," but the webhook fires again, or there's a non-idempotent side effect bolted onto a method that's supposed to be idempotent. The server implementation just isn't honoring the contract.

There's also the classic ambiguous-timeout problem: you send the PUT, the server processes it and commits, but the response never makes it back to you because the network ate it. You don't know whether it succeeded or failed, so you retry. If the server is correctly idempotent, fine, no harm. If it's not — maybe it appends to a list instead of overwriting, or increments a version field as a side effect of any PUT regardless of content — now you've got duplicate effects.

And then there's concurrent modification: two clients PUT the same resource around the same time, your retry lands after someone else's write, and you silently clobber their change. Idempotency protects you against repeating your own call, not against racing other callers. None of this is really PUT's fault, it's usually a gap between what the method promises and what the server actually implements.

turns.question: what's actually in a request header block that the browser adds without me asking for it
turns.answer:
The browser adds several headers on every request. `Host` names the domain, because one server can answer for many domains. `User-Agent` names the browser and the operating system. `Accept` lists the content types the browser can use, in order of preference. `Accept-Encoding` lists the compression formats the browser can decode, such as gzip or br. `Accept-Language` lists the languages the user prefers, from browser settings.

The browser also adds `Connection`, which controls whether it keeps the TCP connection open after this request. It adds `Cookie` when a cookie already exists for this domain. For a cross-origin request, it adds `Origin`, so the server can apply CORS rules. For a request that follows a link or a redirect, it can add `Referer`, which names the page the request came from, though many sites now block this header for privacy.

You can override some of these in code, but the browser sets them by default, and you did not write any of them yourself.
turns.control:
More than people expect. Off the top: Host, which is mandatory in HTTP/1.1 and tells the server which virtual host you want since many sites can share an IP. User-Agent, identifying the browser and OS, partly for compatibility hacks and partly for analytics you didn't opt into. Accept, Accept-Language, and Accept-Encoding, telling the server what content types, languages, and compression (gzip, br, etc.) you can handle.

Then there's the cookie jar — any cookies scoped to that domain and path get attached automatically, which is the whole mechanism behind session auth and also behind a lot of tracking. Connection and Keep-Alive for connection reuse hints, though HTTP/2 multiplexing makes a lot of that moot. Referer, which leaks the page you came from unless the origin's Referrer-Policy says otherwise — this one surprises people the most because it's essentially "here's where I was" sent as a side effect of clicking a link.

On top of that modern browsers add a pile of Sec- and Sec-Fetch- headers: Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Dest, Sec-Fetch-User, which tell the server the context of the request (same-origin navigation vs cross-site fetch vs a script tag) so servers can do their own fetch metadata-based defenses. There's also Sec-CH-UA client hints if the site's opted into them, and If-Modified-Since / If-None-Match when there's a cache entry to revalidate, which is exactly the mechanism we'll probably get into if we talk caching.

turns.question: 301 vs 308, quick, i always forget
turns.answer:
Both mean the resource moved to a new URL, and both are permanent. The difference is what happens to the method and the body on the next request.

A 301 lets the client change the method. In practice, most browsers turn a POST into a GET when they follow a 301, and they drop the body. A 308 keeps the method and the body exactly as the original request sent them.

Use a 308 when the client must resend a POST, a PUT, or a PATCH with its body intact. Use a 301 for a simple page move where a GET is the expected next request anyway.
turns.control:
301 is "permanently moved, and by the way, if this was a POST, feel free to switch to GET when you follow it" — that method-change behavior is legacy and browsers have done it for decades even though it's not really spec-sanctioned, it's just what happened in practice and now everyone depends on it.

308 is "permanently moved, same deal, but preserve the method and body exactly." If you POST and get a 308, the redirect target also gets POSTed with the same body. No silent downgrade to GET.

So: same permanence, different method-preservation guarantee. If you're redirecting a form submission or an API POST and you actually want the client to resubmit with the same method, use 308, not 301, or you'll get bitten by clients that convert it to GET and drop your body. For simple page moves where it's just a GET anyway, it barely matters which one you pick.

turns.question: ok so you mentioned caching headers a second ago and i want to actually nail this down because i've been burned by it before - walk me through the exact decision process a browser goes through between Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified when it's deciding whether it can reuse a cached response or whether it has to go back to the server, and like what order it checks those in if more than one is present at once
turns.answer:
The browser checks freshness first, then validity. These are two separate checks, and it runs them in this order.

Step one: the browser reads `Cache-Control` from the stored response. If `max-age` has not passed, the response is fresh, and the browser uses the cached copy with no network request at all. `Cache-Control` always wins this step over any date-based heuristic.

Step two: if the cached response is stale, or `Cache-Control` contains `no-cache`, the browser must ask the server if the cached copy is still valid. It sends a conditional GET. If the stored response has an `ETag`, the browser sends `If-None-Match` with that value. `ETag` takes priority over `Last-Modified` when both are present, because an `ETag` can detect a change that a timestamp misses.

Step three: if there is no `ETag`, the browser falls back to `Last-Modified`, and it sends `If-Modified-Since`.

Step four: the server checks the condition. A match returns 304, with no body, and the browser reuses the cached copy. No match returns 200, with a fresh body.

`Cache-Control: no-store` skips all of this. The browser never stores the response at all.
turns.control:
Okay, let's actually nail this down properly. There are two distinct phases: freshness and validation, and they're not the same check.

Phase one, freshness: the browser looks at whether it even needs to ask the server anything. Cache-Control is king here — if there's a max-age, the browser computes age (based on the Date header, response time, and any Age header from intermediate caches) and compares it to max-age. If the response is still within max-age, the browser uses it straight from cache, no network request at all, not even a conditional one. Expires is the old-school equivalent of max-age and only matters if Cache-Control isn't present — Cache-Control always wins when both exist. no-cache is a weird trap name: it doesn't mean "don't cache," it means "cache this, but revalidate every time before using it." no-store means actually don't cache it at all.

Phase two kicks in once the cached copy is stale (past max-age) or marked no-cache, or there's no freshness info at all. Now the browser does a conditional GET to revalidate rather than refetching the whole body. If the cached response has an ETag, the browser sends If-None-Match with that ETag value — ETag wins over Last-Modified when both are present, because it's a content hash or version token and is considered more precise. The server compares, and if it matches, it returns 304 Not Modified with no body, and the browser reuses the cached body. If there's no ETag but there is a Last-Modified, the browser sends If-Modified-Since instead, and the server compares timestamps.

So the order is: Cache-Control/Expires decide if you ask at all, then ETag beats Last-Modified when deciding how to ask. Where people get burned is assuming a 304 means "no network request" — it's still a round trip, just a cheap one without the body.

turns.question: why would a cookie marked secure and httponly still get stolen
turns.answer:
Those two flags block two specific paths, not every path. `Secure` stops the browser from sending the cookie over plain HTTP. `HttpOnly` stops JavaScript in the page from reading the cookie through `document.cookie`. Neither flag stops every way to steal a cookie.

A cross-site scripting flaw can still make a request that carries the cookie, even if the script cannot read the cookie's value directly, because the browser attaches the cookie to any request it sends to that domain. The attacker does not need to read the cookie. The attacker only needs the victim's browser to send a request the attacker controls.

A compromised server, a malicious browser extension with request access, or a proxy that terminates TLS and reads the traffic in plaintext can also expose the cookie, because these sit outside the two flags entirely. A stolen device with an unlocked browser session bypasses both flags too, since the browser already holds a valid, decrypted cookie in memory. The flags remove the easy attacks. They do not remove every attack.
turns.control:
Secure and HttpOnly close off two specific attack paths, not all of them, and people treat them like a blanket shield.

Secure just means "only send this cookie over HTTPS, never plaintext HTTP." It stops the cookie from leaking over an unencrypted connection or to a downgraded request, but it does nothing if the connection itself is compromised in some other way — a malicious or misconfigured proxy doing TLS termination, a captured session on a device with a rogue root CA installed, or just a straight-up TLS interception on a corporate network or compromised machine.

HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading document.cookie, which kills the most common XSS cookie-theft pattern. But it doesn't stop an attacker who has XSS from doing damage — they can still issue requests that ride along with the cookie automatically (the browser still attaches it), they just can't read the value directly. So XSS can still be used to make authenticated requests on your behalf, trigger CSRF-like actions, or exfiltrate data through the page itself, even without ever seeing the cookie string.

Other paths that don't care about either flag: malware on the endpoint reading browser storage or memory directly, a vulnerable browser extension with broad permissions, server-side log leakage if the cookie ends up in a URL or gets logged somewhere it shouldn't, or session fixation where the attacker gets you to use a cookie value they already know. Secure and HttpOnly are good hygiene, but they're not the whole session security story — you still want SameSite, short expiry, and ideally rotating tokens on top.

turns.question: ok i need the actual steps: how do i trace a redirect chain from the command line and see every hop with its status code and headers
turns.answer:
Run this command.

```
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null -L -v https://example.com 2>&1
```

`-D -` prints the response headers to standard output. `-o /dev/null` discards the body, because you want headers, not content. `-L` tells curl to follow each redirect. `-v` shows the full request and response for every hop, including the status line.

If you want a shorter view with just the status codes, run this instead.

```
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{url_effective}\n' -L https://example.com
```

This shows only the final status code and the final URL, so add `--trace-ascii -` if you need every hop's headers in one readable log. For a GUI view of the same chain, open your browser's network panel, check "preserve log", and reload the page.
turns.control:
Easiest tool for this is curl with -v or -I chained per hop, or better, just let curl follow and dump each hop's headers. Here's what I'd actually run:

curl -sSL -D - -o /dev/null "https://example.com/start"

-D - dumps headers to stdout, -o /dev/null throws away the body since you don't care about it here, -L follows redirects, -sS keeps it quiet but still shows errors. The problem is this only shows you the final response's headers by default in some curl versions — you want to see every hop's headers, which needs a slightly different approach:

curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null "https://example.com/start" then manually follow the Location header yourself in a loop, or just drop -L and repeat with each new Location until you stop getting a 3xx. That's tedious, so in practice I use:

curl -w '\n---\n' -sSL -D - -o /dev/null --trace-time <url>

Honestly, the tool most people reach for here is httpie with --all, which prints every intermediate response including headers for each redirect automatically: http --all --follow <url>. Or if you want something more visual, there's also curl -v which shows you the full request/response cycle including the TLS handshake, on stderr, per hop, if you don't suppress it. For quick sanity checks I'll also just use a browser's network tab with "preserve log" on, since it shows the whole chain with timing, but command line for scripting it's curl or httpie.

turns.question: alright moving down a layer. what's actually inside the TLS handshake, step by step, and which parts are encrypted vs plaintext
turns.answer:
TLS 1.3 runs the handshake in four round trips worth of messages, and only the first message is plaintext.

Step one: the client sends a `ClientHello` in plaintext. It carries the TLS version, a list of cipher suites, a random value, and a key share for key exchange.

Step two: the server answers with a `ServerHello`, also in plaintext, which picks one cipher suite and sends its own key share. From this point, both sides can compute the same shared secret, so every later message in this same handshake is encrypted.

Step three: the server sends its certificate, a signature that proves it holds the private key for that certificate, and a `Finished` message, all encrypted under the new key.

Step four: the client checks the certificate, then sends its own `Finished` message, also encrypted.

After `Finished` on both sides, the session key is ready, and the application data, meaning your actual HTTP request, travels encrypted from the first byte.
turns.control:
I'll do TLS 1.3 since that's what you're negotiating almost everywhere now (1.2 has an extra round trip and different cipher negotiation, say if you want that version too).

Client sends ClientHello: plaintext. Supported TLS versions, a random nonce, cipher suites, and extensions — critically key_share (the client's ephemeral key exchange material, usually X25519) and server_name (SNI, the hostname, plaintext unless Encrypted Client Hello is set up, which still isn't universal).

Server responds with ServerHello: also plaintext. Its own random nonce, chosen cipher suite, and its own key_share. At this point both sides can independently derive the same shared secret via Diffie-Hellman from the two key_shares, without ever sending the secret itself over the wire. Everything after this is encrypted.

Server sends, encrypted: its Certificate chain, a CertificateVerify (a signature proving it holds the private key for that cert), and Finished (a MAC over the handshake so far, proving no tampering). Client verifies the chain against trusted roots, checks the signature, sends its own encrypted Finished. Application data can start flowing after just one round trip in TLS 1.3 — the server can send data right after its Finished, and there's a 0-RTT mode for resumed sessions sending data with the very first flight, with replay-attack caveats.

So: ClientHello and ServerHello plaintext, SNI visible — exactly the thing you flagged — everything after the key exchange encrypted.

turns.question: wait you said the ClientHello is plaintext - doesn't that leak the hostname i'm connecting to?
turns.answer:
Yes, in most deployments today. The `ClientHello` carries a field named Server Name Indication, which names the hostname the client wants, and this field is plaintext because the server needs it before the handshake can pick the right certificate. A server that hosts many domains behind one IP address cannot pick the correct certificate without it.

Anyone who can see the network traffic, such as your ISP or a network operator on a shared link, can read this field, even though they cannot read the request or the response that follow. This is why a domain name is visible to network observers even over HTTPS, while the URL path and the page content stay private.

A newer extension named Encrypted Client Hello hides the hostname too, by encrypting the SNI field under a key the server publishes in advance. Support is still uneven across browsers and servers, so do not assume it protects you yet.
turns.control:
Yes, it does, and that's a real and fairly well-known privacy gap. SNI (Server Name Indication) has to be sent before the TLS session is established because that's literally how a server hosting multiple sites on one IP knows which certificate to present — if it were encrypted with a key that doesn't exist yet, you've got a chicken-and-egg problem. So historically it's just sent in the clear in the ClientHello.

Practical effect: anyone who can see your network traffic — your ISP, a coffee shop wifi operator, a nation-state intercepting backbone traffic — can see which hostnames you're connecting to even though they can't see what you're doing on those sites or what data is exchanged. They know you connected to example-therapy-site.com even if the actual page content is fully encrypted. This is a meaningfully different privacy leak than full DNS-over-HTTPS solves, because even if your DNS lookups are encrypted, the SNI field in the handshake itself still announces the hostname over the wire.

The fix is Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), which encrypts the ClientHello's sensitive fields including SNI using a public key fetched in advance, usually via a DNS record (HTTPS or SVCB record type) for the service. Cloudflare and some other big CDNs support it, and it's in major browsers now, but wide server-side adoption is still catching up — it needs the DNS infrastructure (usually that means you're behind a CDN advertising ECH keys) and support on both ends. Until it's universal, SNI is effectively metadata leakage baked into how TLS bootstraps itself.

turns.question: what is a certificate chain actually made of and how does a client decide to trust the end one
turns.answer:
A certificate chain is a short list of certificates, each one signed by the certificate above it. At the bottom sits the leaf certificate, issued to the exact domain you are visiting. Above that sits one or more intermediate certificates, issued by a certificate authority. At the top sits a root certificate, which signs the intermediate directly below it.

The client does not trust the leaf certificate on its own. The client checks a signature path from the leaf, up through each intermediate, to a root certificate the client already trusts. The operating system, or the browser, ships with a fixed list of trusted root certificates, and the client only accepts the chain if that path ends at one of them.

The client also checks that each certificate in the chain is within its valid date range, that the leaf certificate's name matches the hostname you asked for, and that no certificate in the chain is revoked. A single broken link in the chain, such as a missing intermediate, causes the whole chain to fail, even when the root is trusted.
turns.control:
A certificate chain is a sequence of signatures, each one vouching for the next. At the bottom is the leaf (or end-entity) certificate — that's the one for the actual domain you're connecting to, containing its public key and the hostname(s) it's valid for. That leaf cert is signed by an intermediate CA's private key. The intermediate cert itself is signed by another intermediate, or directly by a root CA. The root is self-signed — it vouches for itself, which sounds circular, but that's where trust has to bottom out somewhere.

Your OS or browser ships with a trust store — a curated list of root CA certificates that are considered trustworthy by virtue of audits, industry agreements (the CA/Browser Forum), and frankly reputation and liability. When your browser receives the chain during the TLS handshake (leaf plus usually one or two intermediates — roots generally aren't sent, since you're supposed to already have them), it walks the chain upward: verify the leaf's signature using the intermediate's public key, verify that intermediate's signature using the next one up, and so on, until it reaches a cert that matches something already in its trust store. If it gets there, and every signature checks out, and the leaf's hostname matches what you're connecting to, and none of the certs are expired or revoked, the chain is trusted.

If the server forgets to send an intermediate, or sends the wrong one, you get the classic "works in some browsers, not others" problem — some clients cache intermediates they've seen before and can patch the gap, others just fail the chain build entirely.

turns.question: why does my browser trust a cert at all, like who decided these root CAs get to be the ultimate authority
turns.answer:
Your browser or your operating system ships with a fixed list of trusted root certificates, and each one belongs to a certificate authority. These authorities did not appoint themselves. Browser makers and operating system makers each run a root program, a set of rules a certificate authority must meet to stay on that trusted list.

A certificate authority that wants a place on that list must pass an independent audit of its security practices, follow rules set by an industry group named the CA/Browser Forum, and publish every certificate it issues to a public log named Certificate Transparency, so anyone can check what it issued. A browser maker can remove an authority from its list at any time, and this has happened to several authorities after they mis-issued certificates or suffered a breach.

So the trust is not inherent to the certificate authority. The trust comes from a list the browser vendor controls, and that vendor can revoke the whole list entry if the authority fails to meet the rules.
turns.control:
It's not really one authority deciding, it's a somewhat messy ecosystem of trust delegated to operating systems and browser vendors, who each maintain their own root programs. Microsoft, Apple, Google (via Chrome's own root store now, separate from the OS on some platforms), and Mozilla each run a root certificate program with a published set of requirements — audits, key management standards, incident response, revocation capability — and CAs apply to get included. There's also the CA/Browser Forum, an industry group where browser vendors and CAs hash out the "baseline requirements" that all CAs in these programs are supposed to follow.

It's trust by institutional gatekeeping, basically: if you want your root included in Chrome or in Apple's trust store, you go through an audit process (WebTrust or ETSI audits, typically annually) and you're on the hook for following the rules. Screw up badly enough — mis-issue certs, get your private key compromised, lie in an audit — and you get distrusted, which has actually happened to a few CAs over the years (Symantec's sub-CAs being a famous one, distrusted over mis-issuance).

So the honest answer is: you trust root CAs because you trust the browser/OS vendor's vetting process, and that vendor's incentive is that if they trust a bad CA, the security of the entire web depends on it and they'll get burned publicly. It's a reputation-and-liability system more than a cryptographic one — the crypto just enforces whatever trust decisions humans already made.

turns.question: cert expires mid-session vs mid-handshake, what actually happens in each case
turns.answer:
A certificate's expiry only matters at the moment the client checks it, which is during the handshake, not during an open connection.

If the certificate expires mid-handshake, meaning the server presents an already-expired certificate, the client rejects the handshake, and the connection fails before any application data moves. You see a certificate error in the browser, with no page content at all.

If the certificate expires while a session is already open, nothing happens to that session. TLS checks the certificate once, at connection setup, and it does not recheck expiry while the connection stays open. A long-lived connection, such as a persistent WebSocket, can keep running past the certificate's expiry date with no interruption.

The problem appears on the next new connection after expiry. Any client that opens a fresh TLS handshake after that date gets the rejection, even though clients with an already-open connection saw nothing.
turns.control:
Mid-handshake is the straightforward case: the client checks the cert's validity period as part of chain validation, during the handshake. If it's expired at that moment, the handshake fails outright — "your connection is not private," NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID, no connection established. Checked once at setup, that's the gate.

Mid-session is the more interesting case. TLS doesn't re-check certificate validity mid-stream — once the handshake completes, the cert isn't re-verified for the life of that connection, even if it expires a second later. So a long-lived connection (a websocket, a kept-alive HTTP/2 connection, a gRPC stream) just keeps working if the cert expires while it's open. Only the next new handshake sees the expired cert and fails.

This is a genuinely common source of confusing incidents: a cert expires, existing traffic keeps "working fine" for a while since everyone's on already-open connections, then as connections naturally cycle — health checks, reconnects, new users — failures start cascading in. Looks like an intermittent issue before it looks like a hard outage, purely because of when each client's next handshake happens to land relative to the expiry.

turns.question: how would i even notice that a revoked cert is still being accepted somewhere in my stack
turns.answer:
You will not notice it from normal traffic, because a client that accepts a revoked certificate behaves exactly like a client that accepts a valid one. You need to test the check directly.

Run this command against your server.

```
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -status
```

The `-status` flag requests an OCSP response during the handshake, and you can read the result in the output under "OCSP Response Status". If your own client or library never sends this request, it is not checking revocation at all, and no amount of traffic watching will reveal that gap.

Also check your TLS library's configuration directly. Many HTTP client libraries disable certificate revocation checks by default, for performance reasons, so check the library's documentation for the setting name, and confirm it is on. Test it end to end with a certificate you know is revoked, from a service such as a revoked test endpoint, and confirm your client refuses the connection.
turns.control:
This one's genuinely hard to catch because revocation checking is soft-fail almost everywhere by default, which means your stack might be silently not checking at all and you'd have no symptom to notice.

First thing I'd check: does your client even attempt revocation checking? Browsers vary wildly — Chrome mostly relies on CRLSets (its own compressed, curated revocation list, not live OCSP/CRL lookups) for efficiency and doesn't do live OCSP checks by default for most certs. Firefox does OCSP by default but soft-fails if the OCSP responder is unreachable, meaning it just accepts the cert rather than blocking you. So "is a revoked cert being accepted" might just be "yes, because nothing downstream is even asking."

Practically, to actually notice: take the cert in question and manually run the OCSP check yourself rather than trusting the client to surface it — openssl lets you do this directly against the OCSP responder URL pulled from the cert's AIA extension. Compare that against what your actual client stack (your HTTP library, your language runtime's TLS implementation, whatever proxy/load balancer terminates TLS for you) is configured to do. A lot of server-side TLS libraries have revocation checking off by default too, since it adds latency and a dependency on an external service being up.

The other angle: certificate transparency logs and monitoring services (like crt.sh, or a paid cert monitoring tool) won't tell you about acceptance-despite-revocation, but they'll tell you a cert was revoked in the first place, which you need to know before you can even ask whether your stack is respecting it. Practically, the way people actually catch this in the wild is an audit or pentest specifically probing revocation behavior, not organic symptoms — silent acceptance doesn't throw errors.

turns.question: can you give me the actual procedure for pulling a cert off a live server and checking its chain and expiry from the terminal
turns.answer:
Run these three commands, in order.

```
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null > /tmp/chain.txt
```

This saves the full handshake output, including the certificate chain, to a file. The `-servername` flag sends SNI, so a multi-domain server returns the correct certificate.

```
openssl x509 -in /tmp/chain.txt -noout -dates -subject -issuer
```

This fails, because the file holds raw handshake output, not a clean certificate block. Extract the certificate first.

```
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject -issuer
```

This prints the start date, the end date, the subject, and the issuer of the leaf certificate in one pass. Add `-showcerts` to the first command, and pipe the full chain into a separate file, to check every certificate in the chain the same way.

turns.question: ocsp vs crl, practical difference, and why'd everyone mostly give up on one of them
turns.answer:
Both answer the same question: is this certificate revoked? A certificate revocation list, or CRL, is a file a certificate authority publishes that lists every revoked certificate's serial number. A client downloads the whole list and checks if the certificate's serial number appears in it.

The Online Certificate Status Protocol, or OCSP, asks the certificate authority about one specific certificate, and gets back a signed answer for that certificate alone.

Most of the industry moved away from CRLs, because the list grows without a limit, and a large certificate authority's list can reach a size that is slow to download on every check. OCSP avoids the size problem, since each request is small, but it brings its own cost: the client must reach the certificate authority's server on every handshake, which adds delay, and it leaks your browsing pattern to that certificate authority. The current common approach is OCSP stapling, where the server fetches the OCSP answer ahead of time and attaches it to its own handshake, so the client needs no separate network call at all.
turns.control:
Both answer "has this cert been revoked since issuance," just differently. CRL (Certificate Revocation List) is the older approach: the CA publishes a signed list of every revoked cert's serial number, and the client downloads the whole thing and checks if the cert is on it. OCSP is request/response: the client asks the CA's responder "is serial X revoked?" and gets back a signed yes/no/unknown without downloading the whole list.

CRLs don't scale — as CAs issue more certs, lists get huge, and downloading a multi-megabyte list before every connection is a nonstarter. OCSP fixed that with a targeted query instead.

But OCSP has its own problem: it's a live, synchronous dependency on the CA's infrastructure being up, for every handshake. If the responder's slow or down, you either block the connection or soft-fail and accept the cert anyway, which defeats the point — and is what most browsers actually do. It also leaks privacy to the CA, since they see every site you visit via the queries. The fix is OCSP stapling: the server itself periodically fetches its own OCSP response and staples it into the handshake, so the client never contacts the CA directly.

What actually happened: browsers mostly gave up on live CRL or OCSP checks per-connection over latency and availability tradeoffs, and moved to things like Chrome's CRLSets — a compact, curated snapshot of known-bad certs pushed out of band. So it's less "CRL lost to OCSP" and more "both lost to browser vendors rolling their own distribution," with stapling surviving as the well-behaved option where revocation checking still happens properly.

turns.question: ok TCP now. explain the three way handshake but actually explain why it's three, not two or four
turns.answer:
The handshake needs three messages because each side must prove it can both send and receive before data moves.

Step one: the client sends a `SYN` with its starting sequence number. This tells the server the client wants to open a connection.

Step two: the server sends a `SYN-ACK`, which does two jobs in one packet. It acknowledges the client's sequence number, and it sends its own starting sequence number to the client.

Step three: the client sends an `ACK`, which confirms the server's sequence number.

Two messages are not enough, because after step two, the server has not yet heard back from the client, so the server does not know if its own `SYN` reached the client. The third message is that confirmation. Four messages are not needed, because the server's acknowledgment and the server's own `SYN` can travel together in one packet, which is what step two already does. Combining those two is what brings the count down from four to three.
turns.control:
Right, so the three steps are SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Client sends SYN with its initial sequence number. Server responds with SYN-ACK: it acknowledges the client's sequence number and sends its own initial sequence number. Client responds with ACK, acknowledging the server's sequence number.

Why three and not two: TCP is bidirectional from the start — both sides need their own independent sequence number space, since either side can send data once the connection is up. A two-way handshake could establish that the client knows the server's sequence number, but the server would have no confirmation the client actually received its SYN-ACK and is ready to go. You'd be starting a connection where one side doesn't know if the other side is actually listening and synced. Two messages can only prove one direction of "I heard you" — you need a third to close the loop and prove both directions are synced.

Why not four: you could imagine four separate messages — SYN, ACK, SYN, ACK, each side doing its own independent SYN/ACK pair — but TCP is clever here and piggybacks the server's SYN onto its ACK of the client's SYN, into one single SYN-ACK packet. There's no rule that says you can't combine an acknowledgment with your own new sequence announcement in the same packet, so why send two packets when one does the job. That combining is exactly why it's three total flights instead of four — it's not that a fourth step was removed, it's that steps two and three (server's ACK and server's own SYN) were never separate to begin with.

So three is the minimum needed for both sides to prove they've seen and are ready to build on the other's sequence number, with the middle step doing double duty.

turns.question: you said the second step is SYN-ACK combined into one packet - why can those get combined but the final ACK can't also carry data by default without a special case
turns.answer:
The server can combine its `ACK` and its `SYN` into one packet because both flags describe the same packet, not two separate messages. A single TCP packet carries a header with flag bits, and `SYN` and `ACK` are just two bits in that one header, so the server sets both at once, with no conflict.

The client's final `ACK` works differently. By the normal TCP rule, a connection only reaches the `ESTABLISHED` state, where both sides treat data as normal, after that final `ACK` arrives. The server cannot tell, until that `ACK` arrives, that the client is ready to send or receive ordinary data, so sending data before the handshake finishes risks that data arriving at a connection the server has not yet marked open.

A feature named TCP Fast Open is the special case you are thinking of. It lets the client attach data to that final `ACK`, but only after a prior connection already exchanged a cookie that lets the server trust the early data. Without that cookie, the final `ACK` carries no data, by design, so the server only commits to `ESTABLISHED` once it has proof the handshake is complete.
turns.control:
Good catch, and the answer is about what each side is allowed to assume at that point in the handshake versus what it's actually implemented to do by default.

The SYN-ACK combination works because the server, having just received the client's SYN, already has everything it needs to both acknowledge and announce its own sequence number in the same breath — there's no new information it's waiting on, it's just bundling two things it can say simultaneously.

The final ACK could, in principle, carry data — this is literally what TCP Fast Open (TFO) does, piggybacking application data on that third packet to save a round trip. But it's not the default behavior in plain TCP for a few reasons. First, historically, servers couldn't assume it was safe to act on data arriving with the final ACK before the handshake was fully trusted — there's a security angle, since an attacker could spoof SYNs and stuff data into a bare ACK-like packet to try to get a server to process payload before the connection is properly verified, which is part of why TFO needs an explicit cookie mechanism to prevent exactly that kind of abuse. Second, plenty of middleboxes, firewalls and load balancers over the decades have made assumptions about the handshake packets being empty and get confused or drop connections if data shows up early, so it never became safe to rely on universally without an explicit opt-in.

So it's not a hard protocol limitation — it's "allowed by the spec in limited form, but unsafe to do by default without an explicit extension and careful anti-spoofing," versus the SYN-ACK combination, which is just free information bundling with zero extra risk.

turns.question: what is a SYN flood and why does the handshake design make that attack possible in the first place
turns.answer:
A SYN flood is an attack where the attacker sends many `SYN` packets, often with a fake source address, and never sends the final `ACK`. The server answers each `SYN` with a `SYN-ACK`, and then it waits for an `ACK` that never arrives.

The attack works because the handshake design requires the server to hold state after only the first message. The moment the server receives a `SYN`, it must reserve memory for a half-open connection, so it can track that connection while it waits for step three. An attacker can exhaust that memory by opening far more half-open connections than the server can track, and once the table is full, the server refuses every new connection, including requests from real users.

The common defense is a technique named SYN cookies. Instead of storing state for a half-open connection, the server encodes the needed state into the sequence number of its `SYN-ACK` itself, and it only allocates real memory for the connection once the final `ACK` confirms that number. This removes the need to hold state for connections that never complete.
turns.control:
A SYN flood exploits the gap between "received a SYN" and "connection fully established." When a server gets a SYN, it allocates some state for that half-open connection — enough to remember the sequence number and respond with a SYN-ACK — and then waits for the final ACK. That allocated state sits in a queue (the backlog) with a timeout, waiting for a handshake that may never finish.

The attack: send a flood of SYN packets, usually with spoofed source IPs so the SYN-ACKs go out into the void and no ACK ever comes back, and just keep the half-open connections piling up until the server's backlog queue is full. Once it's full, legitimate SYNs get dropped or ignored, because the server has no room left to track new half-open connections. It's a resource-exhaustion attack, not a bandwidth attack — you don't need huge traffic volumes, you need enough SYNs to fill a finite queue faster than entries time out.

The handshake design enables this specifically because step one (SYN) causes the server to commit resources before it has any proof the client is real or reachable — there's no cost or verification required from the sender before the server starts holding state on their behalf. That asymmetry (cheap to send, costly to receive and track) is the whole vulnerability.

The standard mitigation is SYN cookies: instead of allocating real state on the first SYN, the server encodes everything it needs to reconstruct the connection into the sequence number it sends back in the SYN-ACK, cryptographically, and doesn't allocate real backlog state until the final ACK actually arrives with that value echoed back correctly. That way a flood of SYNs that never complete costs the server basically nothing — no memory gets tied up for connections that were never going to finish.

turns.question: flow control vs congestion control, i could not explain the difference to another person right now
turns.answer:
Flow control protects the receiver. Congestion control protects the network.

Flow control stops a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver. The receiver tells the sender, in every packet, how much buffer space it has left, through a field named the window size. The sender never sends more than that window allows, so the receiver's buffer never overflows, no matter how fast the sender can produce data.

Congestion control stops a fast sender from overwhelming the network path between the two hosts, such as a slow link or a busy router. The sender has no direct way to see how busy that path is, so it infers congestion from signals like a dropped packet or a rising delay, and it reduces its own sending rate in response. The receiver's buffer has nothing to do with this decision.

One watches the receiver's capacity. The other watches the network's capacity. Either one can be the limit on how fast data moves, and the real sending rate is the smaller of the two.
turns.control:
Totally fair, they get bundled together because they both throttle how much data gets sent, but they're solving different problems and are signaled differently.

Flow control is about the receiver protecting itself. It's purely between the two endpoints: "don't send me more than I can currently buffer." The receiver advertises a window size (the TCP window) in every ACK, representing how much unacknowledged data it's willing to accept right now based on how full its own receive buffer is. If the receiving application is slow to read data out of the socket buffer, that window shrinks, potentially down to zero (a "zero window" condition), and the sender has to pause until the receiver says it has room again. This has nothing to do with the network in between — it's purely "is the other end of this connection able to keep up."

Congestion control is about the sender protecting the network. It's the sender trying to estimate how much the path between the two endpoints — all the routers and links in between — can handle without getting overloaded, since an overloaded network starts dropping or delaying packets for everyone, not just you. The sender maintains a separate value, the congestion window, that it grows and shrinks based on signals like packet loss or increasing delay, which it interprets as "the network is getting congested, back off." This is inferred, not told to you directly — there's no router sending you a polite "please slow down" message in the base protocol (ECN is an exception but isn't universally deployed), so the sender is guessing based on symptoms.

The actual amount of data the sender can have in flight at once is the minimum of the two windows — receiver's flow control window and sender's congestion window — whichever is smaller wins. Two completely different constraints, same mechanism of "a window that limits in-flight bytes."

turns.question: what's actually happening in slow start, like numerically, window size over the first few round trips
turns.answer:
Slow start grows the sender's congestion window by doubling it roughly every round trip. A sender with a congestion window of 1 maximum segment size sends one segment, and it waits for an acknowledgment. For every acknowledgment that arrives, the window grows by one segment, so after all the acknowledgments for that batch return, the window has doubled.

Round trip one: the window is 1 segment. Round trip two: the window is 2 segments. Round trip three: the window is 4 segments. Round trip four: the window is 8 segments. Round trip five: the window is 16 segments.

This doubling continues until the window reaches a threshold named the slow start threshold, or until a packet is lost. After the threshold, the sender switches to a slower, linear growth, adding roughly one segment per round trip instead of doubling. Growth by doubling is fast, but it also means a loss event near the end of slow start throws away a large window in one step, which is most of why a single loss can cost more than one packet's worth of throughput.
turns.control:
Slow start is TCP's way of probing the available bandwidth without just blasting at max speed and finding out the hard way. It's called "slow" relative to blasting everything at once, but it actually grows fast — exponentially — which surprises people who expect "slow" to mean gradual.

It starts with an initial congestion window, historically small (1-4 segments), but modern TCP stacks (per RFC 6928) typically start around 10 segments, so let's use that as a concrete number. Segment here roughly means one MSS-sized chunk of data, say ~1460 bytes typically.

Round trip 1: send 10 segments. All 10 get ACKed.
Round trip 2: for each ACK received, the window grows by one segment — so 10 ACKs means the window roughly doubles, to 20.
Round trip 3: window doubles again, to 40.
Round trip 4: 80.
Round trip 5: 160.

So it's doubling every round trip, which is exponential growth, not linear — that's the part people miss when they hear "slow start" and picture a gentle ramp. This continues until either a loss is detected (a signal that you've found the network's limit, triggering congestion avoidance, which switches to much slower linear growth) or the window hits a threshold called ssthresh from a previous congestion event, at which point it also switches to the gentler additive-increase behavior.

The reason it starts small and doubles rather than just guessing a big number up front is that you have zero information about the path's actual capacity at the start of a connection, and ramping exponentially gets you to a reasonable estimate within just a handful of round trips rather than either wasting time crawling up linearly or blowing past capacity and causing a pile of loss immediately.

turns.question: why does a single retransmitted packet sometimes tank throughput way more than you'd expect from losing just one packet
turns.answer:
The cost is not the lost packet itself. The cost is what the loss triggers in the sender's congestion control.

When a sender detects a loss, most congestion control algorithms cut the congestion window sharply, often by half, and some older algorithms reset it all the way back to the slow start size of 1 segment. The sender then has to climb back up from that small window, one round trip at a time, before it reaches the throughput it had before the loss. If the round trip time is large, that climb can take seconds, during which the connection sends at a fraction of its earlier rate.

Also, a packet lost out of order can stall every packet behind it. TCP must deliver bytes to the application in order, so a single lost packet holds up every later packet already sitting in the receiver's buffer, even though those later packets arrived fine. The receiver cannot use them until the gap is filled. One lost packet costs one retransmission, but it can cost a window's worth of delay and a slow climb back to full speed.
turns.control:
This is one of those things where the naive mental model — "lost 1 out of 1000, so I lose 0.1% of throughput" — is way off, because TCP's reaction to loss is disproportionate to the loss itself by design.

First, congestion control: a loss is read as "the network is congested." If detected via three duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit), TCP typically halves the congestion window and enters congestion avoidance, growing slowly from there. If detected via a retransmission timeout instead (no duplicate ACKs arrived fast enough, often from a burst of loss), the window gets slammed all the way back to the initial slow-start value and you restart the whole exponential ramp from scratch — a much bigger hit if it trips the timeout path instead of fast retransmit.

Second, head-of-line blocking: TCP guarantees in-order delivery to the application, so if segment 5 is lost but 6 through 20 arrive fine, none of 6-20 get handed up yet — they sit in the reassembly buffer waiting for 5 to be retransmitted. The cost of one lost packet isn't just resending it, it's stalling everything logically after it, even though those bytes already physically arrived.

Third, the retransmission itself takes at least one round trip (detect loss, resend, wait for the ack), and on a high-latency link that dead time alone can dwarf the original packet's transmission cost. Put those three together — window collapse, in-order stall, RTT-bound recovery — and "one packet" can cost an order of magnitude more than its size suggests, especially on long, high-latency pipes where the window was large and had more to lose.

turns.question: give me steps to reproduce packet loss locally so i can actually watch retransmission happen instead of reading about it
turns.answer:
On Linux, use `tc` with the `netem` module.

```
sudo tc qdisc add dev lo root netem loss 5%
```

This drops 5 percent of packets on the loopback interface at random. Run a TCP transfer over that interface, such as `curl` against a local server, while you capture traffic in another terminal.

```
sudo tcpdump -i lo -w /tmp/loss.pcap tcp
```

Open `/tmp/loss.pcap` in Wireshark, and filter on `tcp.analysis.retransmission` to see exactly which packets the sender resent. Remove the rule when you are done.

```
sudo tc qdisc del dev lo root netem
```

On macOS, use the built-in packet filter instead, since `tc` does not exist there. Run `dnctl pipe 1 config plr 0.05`, then add a rule with `pfctl` that directs loopback traffic through that pipe, and capture with the same `tcpdump` command above. The `tc` version is simpler to set up, so test on a Linux VM first if you have one available.

Check it's applied:
tc qdisc show dev eth0

Remove it when done:

You can combine loss with delay to make it more realistic (real loss usually comes with variable latency too):

That's 50ms base delay with 10ms jitter and 5% loss.
